column2: Act One
Birthday Cake Is the Grave of Youth
Birthday Cake is the Grave of Youth

Birthdays did not really matter to Lu Mingfei. Who would remember? His uncle and aunt? Don't be ridiculous. His parents? They were spectacularly unreliable. Was there anyone in the world who actually cared that Lu Mingfei had taken another step toward becoming a sleazy middle-aged man?
A birthday with no one to celebrate it with was just another ordinary day. He had had plenty of those.
He woke to cicadas shrieking their hearts out. The sunshine was almost poisonous, and the stuffy room felt like the steamer in Journey to the West in which demons cooked a fat monk.
Lu Mingfei waved a paper fan inscribed I COME BY MOONLIGHT—words that made him feel like a lecherous thief—and typed www.i-cassell-you.com into his laptop.

He entered the username Ricardo.M.Lu, a password that changed with the date, and authentication from a security USB drive. A tap on Enter refreshed the screen to the Cassell College Vacation Daily Report Form: a dark-green interface with clean, thin borders and more buttons than he could take in at a glance. Lu Mingfei fished a wrinkled little notebook from the pocket of his baggy shorts and began following its instructions item by item.
“Have you detected any unidentified dragons?”

Lu Mingfei checked No. Under a clear blue sky in broad daylight, where would dragons be running around? Coming home for summer vacation meant returning to the real world and severing all contact with reptiles.
“Have you used a Yanling?”

Another No. After the battle at the Three Gorges Reservoir, all his Yanling abilities had vanished again. He had risked a quarter of his life for them, only to get a single use and no after-sales service. Lu Mingze was a crooked businessman.
“Have you experienced any physical abnormalities?”
“Have you discovered any suspected alchemical equipment?”
No, no, no, no, no... This was Lu Mingfei's summer vacation after freshman year. He was doing his daily report.

The daily report was a Cassell College rule. During winter and summer breaks, students had to report online every day. Professors graded the reports: good ones raised a student's GPA, while lying counted as cheating on an exam. In a sense this was their vacation homework, that turd teachers left to spoil your happy days off and remind you they existed. It was like finally getting dessert after a meal, only for someone to sprinkle mustard oil over it. But at Cassell College the daily report was absolutely necessary, because its students were absolutely exceptional.
Cassell College was a private, elite institution for the privileged in the Great Lakes region of Illinois. None of those adjectives quite captured it. It was a paradise for monsters and lunatics.
A college for dragon hybrids.

The professors firmly believed that dragons had once ruled the world as an intelligent race. This rewrote evolution: humanity was no longer the sole pinnacle of the evolutionary tree. Before mammals produced humans, reptiles had given rise to a supreme intelligent species, the dragons. That history had been buried after humanity rose, surviving only in scraps and fragments of ancient myths. But the decline of the dragons did not mean their extinction. The Dragon Kings, bearers of the most sacred bloodlines, merely slept, and would one day awaken. They were unlikely to join the United Nations and build a better home with humanity. They intended to restore the theocratic age of reptiles.

They could do it, too. They were nothing like the monsters of knightly romances, clumsily flying about and stupidly breathing fire. They possessed a mysterious art called alchemy and the sacred power of words known as Yanling, which could even alter the laws of physics.

Most humans believed dragons were only myths because a certain group had long erased evidence of their existence: the dragon hybrids. Born of humans and dragons, they had human hearts and draconic powers. They kept the dragons' secret and bore the duty of guardians. Cassell trained the finest hybrids and sent them around the world to prevent the Dragon Kings' awakening and, when necessary, devise plans to slay them and send those unrepentant monarchs back to their long sleep.

Lu Mingfei had grown up under the red flag and in the sunshine, educated in materialism with all the proper beliefs. Though he sometimes indulged in wild fantasies, he had never imagined supernatural nonsense like dragons could have anything to do with him.
Yet Cassell College had come all that way to recruit him, singing the praises of his bloodline.

The courses were outrageous, and the textbooks even more absurd—more absurd than Japan's new history textbooks. There it was in black and white: humans had not struggled against nature for a million years before learning to use tools and fire; dragons had taught those skills to their servants. Attila the Hun was a dragon, which was why he was so powerful that no one could stop him as he fought his way to Rome. Chinese emperors had not been boasting when they called themselves descendants of dragons, because as far back as the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, every enlightened person fit to lead had indeed been a dragon hybrid...

After taking classes there, Lu Mingfei figured every historical event probably had something to do with dragons. Maybe, just as in Stephen Chow's version of The Deer and the Cauldron, the Qing dynasty had really fallen because the Red Flower Society severed its dragon vein.

Since everyone was a human-dragon hybrid, geniuses were everywhere and elites were a dime a dozen. Every genius and elite had a shocking side, and without strict discipline and management the consequences of letting them run wild were unthinkable. Compared with these hybrids, even Ultraman, Pikachu, and the Transformers might be nothing special. During summer break these people lived among ordinary crowds. If one of them accidentally unleashed a Yanling...
They had indeed learned painful lessons in that regard.

Fortunately, the college leadership were not elegant but useless intellectuals. Before the college was founded, the dragon slayers' organization had been called the Dragon Blood Secret Party. Anyone daring to call themselves a party had to be a scheming customer, no pushover; without an iron hand, how could they command obedience? Principal Anjou therefore played his trump card: the daily report. Students complained, but it worked, reducing accidents that required the college to clean up afterward by as much as eighty percent. Of course, eliminating them entirely was impossible. Last year a student with a heroic streak had secretly taken alchemical equipment from campus to excavate a hidden dragon tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, awakening a dragon about to emerge from its cocoon. He missed his return date and pursued it across thousands of miles, taking Star Alliance flights from Cairo to Istanbul, then New York and Cape Town. Finally, when he fired an alchemical missile at the dragon's seaplane, he shot down a new stealth drone the Pentagon was test-flying. The American stealth-aircraft industry interpreted the incident as proof that an adversary had mastered every technique needed to detect their aircraft and was making an unmistakable demonstration. They abandoned their existing research and threw themselves into a space-shuttle project for attacks from outer space.

The Board of Trustees punished the student severely, but Lu Mingfei had to admit that was how students at Cassell thought: anything went in the pursuit of dragon slaying. The plane had only itself to blame for crossing the senior student's missile trajectory at exactly the wrong moment.

“Mingfei! Don't get up and start playing on the computer first thing! Go downstairs and buy a bag of Cantonese sausage and a bunch of scallions, and check the front desk for any new packages while you're at it!” His aunt's voice carried so well it came through a twenty-centimeter load-bearing wall and left Lu Mingfei reeling. A demonic sound straight through the brain.
“Okay, okay! Just a second!” Lu Mingfei hurried to his feet.

His parents had gone abroad for work when he was little and never returned, leaving him in storage with his uncle and aunt. Only after enrolling at Cassell did he learn they were both distinguished alumni, traveling the world for the cause of dragon slaying and far too busy to look after their troublesome kid. Fortunately, that meant the college viewed him differently and classified his bloodline as S-rank. He was its only S-rank student, with an exclusive scholarship worth tens of thousands of dollars. Admittedly, nobody had seen anything extraordinary about him yet—in other words, everyone else at the college had a Yanling and he did not—but perhaps that could be explained by a modest, understated personality...
After years of swallowing insults in his uncle and aunt's house, he could finally hold his head high. Summer vacation was the perfect time to return home in glory!

He was no longer that troublesome kid. In his first semester's practical course, he had stabbed the King of Bronze and Fire, one of the Four Monarchs of the dragons, to death at the Three Gorges Reservoir... though one might suspect a little cheating.
By comparison, a student ID that doubled as a credit card with a hundred-thousand-dollar limit was nothing. Once you had saved the world, why discuss something as vulgar as money?
He even owned a car now. He had won a Bugatti Veyron in a bet... though he had smashed it up on his first drive and still couldn't afford repairs.

He had a boss, too. He had joined the Student Council under President Caesar Gattuso. Brother Caesar had very few virtues, only three. First, he could fight: with two modified Desert Eagles and Yanling: Kamaitachi, he had actually wounded the Dragon King Constantine. Second, he was rich; Lu Mingfei had won his Bugatti from him. Third, he was generous and grand, spending lavishly every birthday on a swimsuit-and-champagne party by the pool. Few people in the world caught Caesar's eye, yet in front of every Student Council officer he had clapped Lu Mingfei on the shoulder and said, “Recruiting Lu Mingfei is our greatest achievement this year!” His next words were, “Even if he's good for nothing, I won't let our only S-rank fall into Chu Zihang's Lionheart Society!”
What an honor! How could Lu Mingfei not be proud? With that background and status, he had no weaknesses at all!

As the plane crossed the Bering Strait on its way home, Lu Mingfei practiced smiling. No matter how his uncle and aunt praised him, he must smile calmly, not grin and show his gums. That was the aristocratic Cassell style. The passenger beside him watched the boy smile faintly, compose himself, smile faintly again, then compose himself again, over and over as if practicing a secret martial art, and spent the entire journey in terror.

But when he stepped through his uncle's door, he was greeted not by flowers but by a heap of radish strips on the dining table. His uncle and aunt were sweating over a lively operation to pickle dried radish.
“Mingfei, you're back? Perfect timing! Go buy me half a jin of coarse salt!” His aunt was delighted to see him.
“Okay, okay.” From habit, Lu Mingfei put down his luggage, took the two and a half yuan in change, and headed downstairs.
Only outside did it hit him. Damn it! He was practically a successful man now. Did he really have to buy salt himself? Shouldn't his precious hands be reserved for saving the world?
He returned with the salt and helped his aunt cut radishes. Just as he was preparing to describe his year in America with suitable restraint, she spoke first. “Mingfei, let me ask you something...”
He had not yet realized this was the prelude to Cheng Yaojin's three axe blows.
“You've been in America a year. Have you saved any of your scholarship?”

The first blow turned him to stone. She had struck his weak point. On paper he was rich, but the college had strict rules: to collect his scholarship he had to pass every test, submit papers on time, and earn excellent grades. Apart from his practical course, his results were miserable. In twelve months he had received only four months' scholarship money, and his credit card was now thousands in the red. Some of his swagger deflated, and he unconsciously put more effort into cutting the radishes.
“People say American girls are very open. Have you found a girlfriend?” The second blow followed hard on the first.

Lu Mingfei's head dropped. That question really hurt. How could he put it? The figure that kept appearing and disappearing in his heart was... He couldn't very well confess, “I think my boss's girlfriend Nono is great, and she's been good to me, but I'm rather like a toad gazing up at a swan, and I'm still single.”
“Did you see your parents?” The ultimate finishing move.

Lu Mingfei had almost forgotten what they looked like. In a whole year he had received only two letters from his mother, Qiao Weini. Even on the emergency-contact form when he enrolled, he could only put his uncle and aunt. His impressive parents, his dashing parents, his busy parents, the parents who supposedly loved Lu Mingfei so deeply, were occupied with some great enterprise to fight dragons and save the world. They had no time to come back and see him.
In his heart they were as distant as a myth.

You couldn't always ask someone else to say “I love you” for you, could you? Even if you wrote it a thousand times in letters, one day you still had to say it yourself. Lu Mingfei wanted his parents to prove their sincerity one day, with something dramatic: suddenly appearing before him, travel-worn, suitcases in hand, standing amid steam from a train or the rush of air behind a plane, gazing silently at their troublesome son and saying in trembling voices, “You've... grown so much?”
Right? That would be moving! Then he could resist the urge to crouch on the ground and bawl, and say casually, “You're back.”
Come on, heroes! Prove to the unlucky kid you brought into this world that you would cross mountains and oceans just to see him and say a sentimental “I love you”!
But so far, to Lu Mingfei, his parents were merely signatures at the ends of letters, definitions in a figure of speech, and two splendid names in an alumni directory: Lu Lincheng and Qiao Weini.
Lu Mingfei fell silent. His knife struck hollowly against the chopping board.

His aunt understood at once. With a contemptuous smile she said she'd known his parents were unreliable. She had hoped they might recommend Mingze, but fortunately she'd had the foresight not to wait. If she had relied on them, would Mingze ever have gotten into Austin University?

His cousin Lu Mingze had just received his acceptance from Austin University, and the whole family had celebrated. After spending a year in the shadow of “even a loser like Lu Mingfei got into an American university,” his aunt could finally hold her head high. Her back straightened, her legs stopped aching when she walked, and she could speak without running out of breath. An American university acceptance letter worked like a calcium supplement for her.
“Don't cut the strips so thick! The salt won't get in!” his aunt barked.
“Mm-hmm.” Lu Mingfei was sweating buckets.

“Apply to our Austin University. It's a famous school, everyone's very friendly, and the professors are especially nice...” Lu Mingze's voice came from the inner room. Wearing a headset, he was chatting on QQ voice with his feet on the desk and the air conditioning turned up high. Cool air bathed him, and a girl's soft admiration at the other end sent him floating, lending his voice ever more dramatic rises and falls. He was 160 centimeters tall and weighed 160 jin, but when it came to chasing girls he was far more reliable than his cousin. He had heard his cousin was still single; if he got a girlfriend first, he would be what his mother called a winner in life.

Actually Lu Mingze had no real need to look down on Lu Mingfei. With Austin University behind him, he felt superior to his cousin from head to toe in every possible way. But since he was so outstanding, he might as well show off without shame.
To the clatter of the keyboard, Lu Mingfei packed the radish strips into a pickle jar, rubbed coarse salt over each layer, and sealed it. Salt seeped into his skin, leaving it dry and rough.
“Carry the jar out to the balcony! Look how clumsy you are. You didn't learn to cook in America either, did you?” His aunt pointed.

Among the most invincible creatures in the world were middle-aged women: sturdy, practical, and sharp-eyed. With only three questions they could reduce a swaggering brat to his true form. To a middle-aged woman, if you had no parents, girlfriend, or money, what were you showing off for? However capable you were, however many dragons you'd killed, it meant nothing. Even if you were great enough to master Star Platinum, you still needed a reason to throw a punch, didn't you? You had nothing, not even a reason to throw a punch... Were you supposed to fight for eternal justice?
What nonsense.
“Hurry up! How long have I been calling you? Lazy and poor go together, ever heard that? If you're lazy, you'll be poor!” His aunt grew sharper still.

Lu Mingfei hastily clicked Send and rushed out. His aunt's demonic voice boring through his brain... even a hero like his uncle, who had practiced the Golden Bell Shield for twenty years, couldn't withstand it.
“Ricardo.M.Lu, you have one unread message.” A window suddenly appeared on the screen.
Ricardo:
According to your enrollment information, you were born on July 17, 1991, and turn nineteen today.
On this important day, on behalf of Principal Hilbert Jean Anjou and all the professors of the academic board, I wish you a happy birthday.
Thank you for attending Cassell College and sharing these wonderful times with us. It is an honor to grow together.
Yours sincerely, Norma.

PS. Under college rules, a student celebrating a birthday may collect one birthday cake from the cafeteria. Since you are currently on summer vacation in China, your complimentary birthday cake has been canceled. Furthermore, the summer term begins July 20, 2010. Your transcript shows D grades in two courses last semester, meaning you did not pass. I regret to inform you that you must attend remedial classes and retake the examinations during the summer term. I have booked your flight back to campus. Please be ready to depart at any time.

“Birthday?” Lu Mingfei stared. Since coming home, he had spent his days serving at his aunt's command and his evenings playing StarCraft. The days had blurred together, and he had completely forgotten.

He was nineteen, just like that? Time really flew. Think of what heroes had accomplished at nineteen... Zhou Yu and his sworn brother Sun Ce had already established a base in Jiangdong and married the Qiao sisters, with territory and women to call their own... And this was how his own nineteenth birthday arrived?
“What the hell? What kind of congratulatory email is this? It's just telling me my free cake is canceled and I failed classes!” After reading the PS twice, Lu Mingfei finally caught on.

Birthdays did not really matter to Lu Mingfei. Who would remember? His uncle and aunt? Don't be ridiculous. His parents? They were spectacularly unreliable. Was there anyone in the world who actually cared that Lu Mingfei had taken another step toward becoming a sleazy middle-aged man?
A birthday with no one to celebrate it with was just another ordinary day. He had had plenty of those.
His phone chimed. A text had arrived.
“Happy birthday. Chu Zihang.” As concise as that senior student's expressionless face.
Someone actually remembered his birthday, and that someone was Chu Zihang.

Chu Zihang was president of Cassell's Lionheart Society, the Student Council's sworn enemy, while Lu Mingfei was a new Council member. It was like Lu Su waking on his birthday to a card from Cao Cao: bewildering and full of conflicting feelings. Lu Mingfei had no idea how Chu Zihang had gotten his number. He certainly hadn't saved Chu Zihang's, and the senior had spoken fewer than a hundred sentences to him altogether. Was this an attempt to win him over? But would the stone-faced senior, who would cut down anyone who stood in his path, really resort to such tactics?
While Lu Mingfei was speculating, another text arrived.
“Lu Mingfei, is this your number? I'm Chen Wenwen. The Literature Club is having lunch at Sophie Lad Pizza at 11:30 today. Come along if you get this.”
His heart rippled... No, a colossal meteorite had struck the middle of the Pacific, raising towering waves!

The sudden message was like Chen Wenwen's invitation to join the Literature Club years ago: casual, unexpected, and delightful. That had been a summer too. Cicadas screamed their hearts out, the sunlight outside was blinding, and the shadow of the eaves lay sharp as a blade across the ground. He had leaned against the windowsill, bored out of his mind, while Chen Wenwen, in a blue-and-white cloth dress and low-heeled sandals, moved lightly past as though walking on tiptoe along a road at night.
“Are you Lu Mingfei? Do you like reading?” Chen Wenwen had stopped abruptly.
He had looked up in surprise. Her eyes were like water, rippling faintly as they reflected the sun.
“Pathetic,” Lu Mingfei muttered. Chen Wenwen had a boyfriend now, and the whole affair had left him miserable... Yet remembering that instant when he looked up still stirred him.
“Sure,” he replied.
“Mingfei, you haven't left yet?” His aunt burst in.
“I'm going, I'm going!” Startled, Lu Mingfei snapped to attention.

“Good thing you haven't.” She waved what she was holding: a cracked toilet seat. “Your uncle cracked it sitting on it. Go to the building-supply market and buy a new one, beechwood, something decent. Your uncle and I are taking Mingze to buy a suit for going abroad, to wear at the graduation ceremony! Don't dawdle. Buy the seat and have the property management people install it. We'll be back at four thirty this afternoon. Steam the sausage, clean the scallions, and cut some radish for soup!”
Having issued her orders, his aunt turned and left. The outer door slammed, and a few minutes later his uncle's little BMW drove away downstairs.
Lu Mingfei's head ached. What a busy birthday: the Literature Club gathering, his aunt's many errands, and a family dinner that evening to celebrate Lu Mingze's departure for study in America.
Eleven time zones away, at Cassell College in Illinois.

Late at night the central control room on the library's second floor was ablaze with light. Manstein stood before a giant 3D projection: a virtual globe five meters high floated before him, spinning rapidly to whatever location he wanted with a light wave of his hand. It felt like a god manipulating his creation, a thrilling sense of command and power. If politicians knew such an advanced projection system existed, they would scramble to buy one and indulge their urge to direct the world: cosplay Hitler if they liked, Genghis Khan if they preferred, like the old teacher in From the Herbal Garden to the Three Flavor Study reciting of an iron scepter wielded in splendid command and golden cups emptied without drunkenness.
But Manstein was not enjoying himself at all. Manstein wanted to die.

Seven or eight red lights flashed at once on the ghostly blue globe, alarms rising and falling. The control room was filled with rapid keyboard clatter, printers hissing, and mechanical cipher machines clicking as they translated coded messages. His head was ready to explode. Day or night, the atmosphere was always like this; tonight Manstein was the unlucky professor on duty.

As many as seventy experts and interns worked there, each facing several terminals at once. The college secretary, or rather the supercomputer named Norma, gathered information relevant to the college from across the world, but people still had to analyze it and make decisions. The central control room was the college's think tank.

“Executive Department agents intercepted a smuggling plane over Peru. We found priceless Egyptian alchemical equipment dating from 700 BC in the cabin! They have the situation completely under control,” an intelligence officer shouted hoarsely through his headset. “But they shot the plane down... They're making an emergency landing and requesting rescue!”
“Please sign this reimbursement form. Our agents in Greece are waiting for the funds!” A female secretary hurried up in clicking high heels and handed Manstein a bill.
“Seventy thousand dollars?” His eyes bulged. “For a sum this large they need to submit a formal report!”
“There's no time... They're dealing with the mob.”
“We're a college! We're educators! What are we doing dealing with the mob?” Manstein exploded.

“Several recent serial murders are suspected to involve a death servitor. The mob knows something, and our agents in Greece believe it must be captured before the police get involved.” The secretary caught her breath. “It's urgent. They called directly for money. Both sides reportedly have their fingers on their triggers while they wait. If the money doesn't arrive... the other side may think they're being cheated and open fire!”
Manstein was about to say more when an anxious financial expert rushed over.
“OPEC announced an increase in crude oil prices five minutes ago!”
“What the hell do crude oil prices have to do with me?” Manstein glared. “I didn't buy oil futures.”
“But the college did... a huge position, using over 1.2 billion in reserves. If we don't sell in time, we'll suffer enormous losses.”
“How enormous?” Manstein covered his face.
“Conservatively, possibly two hundred million...” The expert wiped cold sweat from his face.
Manstein felt one breath away from spraying blood all the way to the ceiling. He signed the secretary's bill with a flourish, turned to the financial expert, and ordered, “Sell! Sell everything!”

He couldn't be bothered about Greece's seventy thousand dollars. Tonight a word from him moved hundreds of millions; was there any point getting angry over a mere seventy thousand? What a wretched night, and he alone had to hold it together. Normally three professors shared a shift: tonight it was his turn with Guderian and Schneider, director of the Executive Department. The scatterbrained Guderian was plainly unreliable, so when he said he was used to going to bed early and didn't want overtime, Manstein agreed to cover for an old friend. But Schneider, famed as an iron-willed enforcer, had let him down too, saying he had an important academic paper to revise and asking Manstein to cover. Manstein knew that although Schneider was a butcher—he regarded everyone in the Executive Department as butchers, crude people who knew only knives and guns—he had always wanted more publications so he wouldn't fall behind the other professors academically. So he agreed.
But the whole world was unsettled tonight, and not one piece of good news had arrived to lift his spirits.
“The Equipment Department has achieved tremendous success testing a new alchemical weapon in the Sahara!” An intern sprang from his chair and raised his arms in triumph.

His wild delight caught on. Everyone knew the department was preparing a secret weapons test deep in the Sahara: a superweapon that might tip the balance between humans and dragons. It had succeeded! Everyone raised their arms and cheered, as if NASA had just announced a successful moon landing.

Manstein perked up and started toward the intern's terminal. Then a piercing alarm swept through the control room. It was a high-level warning. He turned to see a rapidly flashing red light expanding in the heart of the Sahara on the globe, threatening to engulf the entire earth!
“What happened? Didn't you say it was a tremendous success?” he roared at the intern.

“A minor problem... The Pentagon's spy satellite Tungusta happened to be passing over the Sahara and observed our test. It mistook it for... a nuclear explosion. According to our inside source, the CIA has reported it to the president. Since the test site was in Libya, the ambassador there will probably issue a stern diplomatic note very soon... accusing Libya of conducting a secret nuclear test...”
Manstein slapped himself hard. I knew it, he thought. When has that bunch of lunatics in the Equipment Department ever brought good news? But did they have to make it this outrageous?
“What alchemical weapon could possibly be mistaken for a nuclear explosion?” the duty professor cried in anguish, his voice echoing through the library's marble corridors.

“A tactical missile fitted with an alchemically refined silver warhead... Combined with refined mercury, niter extracted from Vesuvius's volcanic ash, and the blood of a holy infant, the explosion can lethally poison dragons in its central zone.”

“What use is that? How many dragons will wait in the middle of the desert for you to bomb them? What if one is in New York? Kill thousands of people along with one dragon? Those ingredients can kill humans as well!” Manstein collapsed into his chair. “I need to make some calls to deal with this... I need a little time...” Then he sprang up again, slamming both palms on the desk. “Executive Department, send people immediately! People! Fly them to the Sahara and clean up the site before the Pentagon gets there!”

A tremendous roar drowned him out. The floor shook violently and the lights went out, then came back on. Manstein fell, rolled to his feet, and rushed to the window. A column of dark-blue flame shot into the night sky from the direction of the Ice Cellar, the storehouse for alchemical equipment. The things kept there could destroy the earth several times over!
“Something's happened!” He lunged for the central console and grabbed a hammer to smash the glass covering the red lever for the campus-wide alarm.

Then the red telephone on the console rang. He hesitated, but answered it first. The line went directly to the Ice Cellar; he wanted to find out what was happening. Intruders? An accidental explosion?
“Hello? Who's on duty tonight?” asked a casual voice.

“Manstein, head of the Discipline Committee! What's going on?” The tone infuriated him. He recognized the Equipment Department's spokesperson. The weapon-obsessed lunatics rarely appeared in person and entrusted their communications to this unreliable representative.

“Just a routine experiment, a tiny bit of open flame. Everything is under our control,” the spokesperson said calmly. “No need to make a fuss. We're calling to notify you that the Equipment Department has an experiment in the Ice Cellar tonight.”
Manstein's eyes blazed. “Under control? Your Sahara experiment...”
“All departments in position! Hydrogen flame ready. Let's do it again...” someone called through the receiver.
“Again? You lunatics won't stop until somebody gets killed, will you?” Manstein roared, but only a busy signal answered. The spokesperson had already hung up with brisk efficiency.

He slowly replaced the receiver and sank weakly into his chair. What could he do? Some departments at the college could not be offended, and Equipment was one of them. Even knowing their reckless experiments might bring the sky down... no one wanted their new equipment to explode for no reason on the next assignment.

Quick, sharp footsteps approached and the control-room door was shoved open. Schneider was dragging Guderian along. These two disloyal fellows had left Manstein to take the blame alone; ordinarily they would hardly return out of kindness. Guderian had apparently been dragged from his nest and was still wearing a Pikachu nightcap. Entirely in keeping with his taste.

“What is it?” Manstein snatched off Guderian's cap and tossed it aside, but addressed Schneider. Guderian looked sleepy, with an expression that said this had nothing to do with him and he wanted to go back to bed.
“We lost some information in China.” Schneider's voice was low and hoarse, always enough to make a listener's skin crawl.

“Tsk!” Manstein scoffed. What was one lost document in China? One of them had gone to sleep in a Pikachu cap, the other had used a paper as an excuse, and he had been left alone for twelve hours. In that time he had cleaned up after seven Executive Department teams around the world, authorized as much as $120,000 in expenses, prevented a gunfight, and was dealing with an imaginary nuclear crisis... And now they rushed in to tell him some information was lost?

Schneider slapped a file onto the desk. The dark-red stamp on its cover brought Manstein's overtime-muddled brain awake as if someone had poured cold water over it. It showed a great serpent holding its tail in its mouth to form a circle, its scales distinct, with two bold black letters in the center: SS.
“Top classification...” Manstein said softly.

Cassell missions, like bloodlines, were divided into grades. In descending priority they were A, B, C, D, E, and F. Special missions beyond those grades were designated S-rank. S-rank missions were rare; Operation Bronze against the Dragon King Norton at the Three Gorges Reservoir had been one. SS was an exception among exceptions, not necessarily more important than S but extraordinarily special. Such missions came directly from the Board of Trustees, bypassing Principal Anjou.

The nuclear crisis had just been classified A-rank and had already reached the diplomatic level, yet the mission involving this information was SS. What could be so deadly important that even the trustees hidden behind the scenes couldn't sit still? Some scandal involving the trustees?
“Yes. Something the board wants.” Schneider nodded slowly.
Manstein nodded and clapped his hands. “Ladies and gentlemen, give us the room.”
Everyone else stood and filed out. As the financial expert passed Manstein, he asked quietly, “Sell in stages?”

“That's not important now. Decide for yourself.” Manstein waved him away, leaving the 1.2-billion-dollar transaction to the expert. Only one thing mattered now: an SS-rank mission. Once one appeared, everything else gave way.
“You can't leave!” He caught Guderian trying to slip out at the back of the line and pulled him back.
“You said you wanted to talk alone,” Guderian said, scratching his head. “I don't understand those things you're discussing anyway.”
“But you're a professor on duty.” Manstein sighed. “None of us can decide an SS-rank mission alone. With the principal away, the duty professors decide together. You have to be here.”

Only the three of them remained in the vast control room. The doors closed tightly. No one dared eavesdrop on a secret mission from the trustees; the college might have a free atmosphere, but its rules were strict.
“What is it?” Manstein asked.

“You're better off not asking,” Schneider said. “You weren't supposed to know anything about it. It was handled directly by the Executive Department. We only had to tell you because something went wrong.”
“With a mission classified this highly, the Executive Department should have given it everything. How could there be a problem?”

“We did give it everything. We made detailed plans, obtained the information, and sent our best man to escort it back to campus personally. But it was lost on the way.” Schneider gestured. The projection changed to a building with a turtle-shell-shaped glass dome, like an airport waiting hall, except it had been completely deformed. Its high-strength aluminum-alloy beams were twisted like pretzels. A simulation showed the disaster: as the ground shook, every beam twisted inexplicably, as if turned by giant hands, and thousands upon thousands of glass panes broke loose and fell straight down.
“I've seen that hall. It's the South Railway Station!” Guderian said suddenly.

“Yes. You saw it in Lu Mingfei's hometown. It was still under construction when you went for the interview, and began trial operations this summer. Its glass dome consisted of 3,200 high-strength panes, and its aluminum frame was designed to withstand a magnitude-eight earthquake, using the most advanced building technology. But this morning, Beijing time, it was destroyed in a magnitude-three quake. All 3,200 panes fell vertically, like 3,200 blades cutting at once.” Schneider paused. “And our man was waiting for a train there with the information.”
“He died?” Manstein asked.
“Cut to pieces,” Schneider said quietly. “It was Raymond.”

They had deployed Agent B007, Raymond, which showed how careful the Executive Department had been. A 2006 graduate of Cassell's mechanical engineering department, B-rank, Raymond possessed Yanling number 28, Blazing Sun, radiating light up to 4,000 lumens within his domain. The light could not kill, but his domain was a giant incandescent bulb fifty meters across. Anyone approaching him effectively entered the bulb and couldn't open their eyes. Though not a high-level Yanling, it was considered absurdly powerful, a game-breaking ability. Yet Raymond had died, and Blazing Sun had been useless, because his opponents had no eyes: 3,200 panes of glass falling from the sky.
“The casualties must have been terrible,” Manstein said.
“Besides Raymond, only three people were injured. The station was still in its trial period, with few departures and few passengers waiting.”
“Was he attacked by one of our kind? A building designed to withstand a magnitude-eight quake collapsing in a magnitude-three one is impossible to explain,” Manstein said.
“I know. In China they call that tofu-dreg construction,” Guderian interjected.
“If you don't understand, stop squawking!” Manstein snapped. “A magnitude-three quake wouldn't even bring down a condemned building!”

“We don't know. I've never heard of a Yanling like that,” Schneider said. “What Yanling could destroy an aluminum-alloy hall large enough for thousands of passengers? That kind of force is almost comparable to Rhine.”
“We don't have time to send an investigation team, do we?” Manstein said.
“No investigation team. Send someone to recover the information directly. The board's deadline is seven tonight, local time.” Schneider checked his watch. “About eight hours.”
“Who can we send? Who's nearby? Dispatch someone local.”

“People in other cities can't make it. Railways and airports are closed until nine tonight against aftershocks,” Schneider said. “The campus maintenance staff could drive there; they have a group vacationing in China.”
Manstein pictured those men with steel-hard arms and stone-slab chests and shook his head. “Maintenance can assist, but the agent should have a bloodline advantage.”
“Then we can only call on students: A-rank Chu Zihang and S-rank Lu Mingfei. Both have an unquestionable bloodline advantage,” Schneider said. “Their homes are local, and they're on summer break.”

Even in this serious, tense moment that admitted no levity, Manstein gave a rueful smile at Lu Mingfei's name. A bloodline advantage? He had one, certainly; S-rank marked the highest bloodline. But...
“That's right! With Mingfei there's no problem! He's S-rank!” Guderian looked as though he'd found treasure in a garbage heap. As Lu Mingfei's adviser, he had always had confidence in his student.

“I really don't know where your confidence comes from. Your S failed two courses last semester; the transcript has already gone to the academic board.” Manstein shook his head. “An S-rank who can't even use a Yanling. Without a Yanling he has no innate ability. As a hybrid he's useless.”
“Send Chu Zihang,” Schneider said. “He has successfully completed many missions.”

“As head of the Discipline Committee, I'm responsible for student discipline, and there are things I remember very clearly. Your student Chu Zihang is a confirmed devotee of violence. His record contains twelve disciplinary citations for violent tendencies during missions!” Manstein shook his head again. “Put an ungraduated violent offender in charge of an SS-rank mission?”
“The Executive Department is itself an organization of violence!” Schneider was just as protective of his own student.
“I know you're the chief thug,” Manstein said. “But no. Chu Zihang can't be in charge alone.”
“We have no choice,” Schneider said. “I know my student. Chu Zihang is suited to working alone.”
“He doesn't have to go alone. Mingfei will support him!” Guderian seized the opportunity.

Manstein looked straight into Schneider's iron-gray eyes. “A top-level mission needs a top-level team. Chu Zihang does have a bloodline advantage, but he isn't good enough to carry out a mission of this level by himself. At most he can be one member of a team!”
“I head the Executive Department. This is its mission, and Chu Zihang is my student. Do you understand?” Schneider was just as forceful.
“There's Mingfei...” Guderian watched their gazes strike sparks.
After several seconds, Schneider and Manstein both realized neither could overwhelm the other. They turned simultaneously and paced apart in agitation.
“Mingfei...” Guderian looked from one to the other.

“Chu Zihang as agent! Lu Mingfei assisting!” Schneider and Manstein turned and spoke at once. At last they had compromised. They had no choice: time was running out, and no one could afford to offend the trustees.

“Norma, inform the board of the team roster,” Schneider said, thrusting his fingers into the projection and moving them rapidly to summon information. “We're drawing up an operational plan and will report to them promptly.”
“Understood.” An elegant female voice came from speakers on all sides.

“The board has replied. The team is to be adjusted: S-rank Lu Mingfei is appointed agent for this mission, with A-rank Chu Zihang assisting him. Chu Zihang is to follow Lu Mingfei's direction.” Several minutes later, Norma's voice came again from overhead.
All three duty professors froze. For a long time the control room was silent.
“My God! The board really does recognize Mingfei's talent!” Guderian pressed both hands to his chest in delight.

Manstein and Schneider both raised hands to their foreheads, perhaps checking for fever and wondering whether they were hallucinating. They knew exactly what the college's only S-rank Lu Mingfei was: a “gifted student” struggling on the verge of remedial exams; a loser who would have been demoted without the principal's unconditional protection; an unpredictable wild card who lost his nerve when needed and stunned everyone when he wasn't supposed to appear. Put someone like that in charge? Let him command the elite of the elite, Chu Zihang, president of the Lionheart Society, who had completed twelve missions without a single failure? How was that different from asking Cassell's number-one loser Fingel to solve the Sahara nuclear crisis? Were they trying to destroy the earth?
Morning sunlight poured through the skylight onto the empty basketball court. A ball struck a bright patch with a soothing thump, thump. Chu Zihang was alone, dribbling, crouching, breathing deeply.

An electronic whistle sounded across the court. Chu Zihang moved, driving forward with the ball, leaping like a hurricane, and dunking! His body blurred with speed, and the ball struck the floor so rapidly it sounded like automatic gunfire.

The ball never reached the floor. Chu Zihang landed first and caught it, then immediately turned, drove toward the other basket, and dunked again! The hoop gave a tremendous crack, as though it might break.
He repeated the cycle, the electronic scoreboard rolling upward. It was a basketball game with one player, but both sides' scores rose in turn.

The final whistle sounded, and the scoreboard reached 50–50. His shoes hissed sharply against the floor as he slid into the center circle and slowly straightened. Only then did the ball land with a thump at one side of the court.
Until that moment he had not shed a drop of sweat. A few seconds later it poured out as though a sluice had opened, soaking his jersey.

This was the basketball court in Chu Zihang's home; he was doing his morning exercise. In middle school he had played center on the city's youth team, but after his bloodline awakened, most human competitive sports became dull. Greater muscular strength, superior agility, and bones able to bend beyond ordinary angles meant playing basketball against normal people was now like golf: pure recreation. Few people at Cassell liked basketball. Even the girls could leap and dunk easily, making the game uninteresting. Intellectual contests such as go and sports such as downhill skiing, which tested agility and courage, were popular. No one wanted to play games won simply by brute strength.

So he could only play against himself, turning an enjoyable sport into monotonous morning exercise. Caesar always mocked his taste in sports. Caesar naturally preferred Cassell's classic pastime of sailing: noble and carefree, well-shaped arms drawing substantial ropes, cold water splashing against a bare chest as the boat sped across great lakes and oceans.
Chu Zihang kept playing basketball. He had never been an interesting person anyway.
That man had been the first to teach him basketball. That alone was enough reason to keep playing for life.

Chu Zihang jumped out of his red jersey and went into the shower. Even showering followed a procedure: exactly three minutes, one minute hot, one cold, one warm. The hot water drove out the remaining sweat; the cold tightened muscles and skin; the warm rinsed him clean before he left. While Caesar and the Student Council officers soaked in a petal-strewn whirlpool bath drinking beer, they often joked that if they were living in decadent ancient Rome, Chu Zihang was a medieval ascetic.
Caesar was not quite right. Chu Zihang did not enjoy hardship; he simply wanted to remain as precise as a machine.

Cold water flowed over his raised muscles like streams through mountain rocks. Muscles and tendons overheated by exercise slowly returned to normal. He breathed in and out rhythmically, slowing his heartbeat and blood flow. His physical training specialty was tai chi.
Then his phone, sealed in a waterproof bag, rang. He never let it leave his side, even in the shower.
“I have a mission for you.” His adviser Schneider always spoke in commands, blunt as a club descending on one's head.
“I'm listening.” Chu Zihang quickly dried himself.

“Urgent mission, SS-rank. Recover important information before seven tonight. Norma has emailed you the detailed instructions.” Schneider paused and lowered his voice. “Exercise restraint... Don't make the scene too big. Avoid casualties as far as possible. Don't be like those lunatics in Equipment...” A faint explosion came through the receiver, and Schneider's voice filled with anger. “They're dismantling the campus!”
“SS?” Chu Zihang was uninterested in the Equipment Department's lunatics. It was the mission's classification that surprised him. The highest he had previously taken part in was A-rank.
“You heard correctly. You were originally scheduled to return to campus today, weren't you? Norma has booked you and Lu Mingfei on tonight's UA836 nonstop to Chicago.”
“Lu Mingfei?” Chu Zihang was taken aback.

Schneider paused. Even a man as hard and blunt as he found this arrangement difficult to announce and had to choose his words. “The agent in charge is S-rank Lu Mingfei. Your job is to assist him. You are to follow his instructions.”

Chu Zihang was confused. What did that mean? An emperor summons his great general and says he wants him to go north against the barbarians with Chief Palace Eunuch Lu. The general naturally knows Eunuch Lu is there as an overseer: the general does the fighting, the eunuch takes the credit, and the general can only thank the emperor and obey. That would be normal. What was abnormal was the emperor saying, I'll give Eunuch Lu armor, a sword, and a fine horse so he can charge in front, while you run logistics behind him... Wasn't that a plan to get Eunuch Lu killed?
“Understood.” Chu Zihang's tone remained calm. He was not one to argue.

After hanging up, he opened his wardrobe. A long black tennis bag lay in the corner. He unzipped it to reveal a sword hilt wrapped in black rayskin, pressed against a racket. He took the hilt and drew the blade an inch. Iron-blue light flashed, and a chill ran swiftly up his wrist.

The sacred sword Murasame, the demon blade said to produce spring rain after killing, washing away the blood. Someone had cast this nonexistent sword from regenerated metal and enshrined it for ten years to cultivate its murderous aura.
“Did you get your Birkin? I've been on the waiting list for two years. Do you think they only sell them to VIPs?”

“I did. Last time I went to Europe, I bought tens of thousands of yuan worth of little things at Hermès, and the clerk quietly told me they had one in stock. I grabbed it without thinking. But it's alligator skin, and the pattern isn't very pronounced.”
“Show-off! You're lucky to get one. When are you going to lend it to me?”
“Give me a kiss, pretty lady, and I'll reward you.”
“Drop dead!” A woman curled up on the sofa kicked at the woman opposite with bare feet, which the other caught.

Four women of auntie age giggled, their hair disheveled, makeup smeared, rolling around on the sofa in silk nightgowns and drinking black tea to recover from their hangovers. Last night's three bottles of cognac had been powerful enough to knock them all out, and they had slept in this state at Chu Zihang's home until the sun was high.
“It's nearly noon. What are we eating?” Someone suddenly felt hungry.

The door opened silently and a tall, slender boy walked in, glancing at the cans scattered across the floor and the four women who had been famous throughout the city for their beauty when young. He frowned. “What a mess. Couldn't you ask Auntie Tong to help clean up?”
“Oh, Zihang, you're so handsome! Come sit with Auntie a while,” Auntie Shanshan said happily.
Chu Zihang wore faded blue jeans and a white T-shirt, simply dressed, with the black tennis bag across his body and the scent of freshly washed sandalwood in his hair.

He was no longer a little boy, but a genuine male. The beautiful aunties had no notion of being modest around him: graceful legs sprawled as before, slim waists twisted as before. They had watched him grow up. His mother had been the first of their circle to have a child, and the aunties adored this toy fallen from heaven. His early memories were traumatic: at two or three, enveloped in perfume and powder, scarlet lips all around, aunties competing to carry him and long elegant hands pinching his little bottom...
“I can't stay. I ordered food for you: two eel rice bowls and two teriyaki beef rice bowls,” Chu Zihang said. “They'll be here soon.”
“How thoughtful!” The aunties' eyes sparkled. Chu Zihang remembered what each of them liked to eat.

He looked at his mother, curled on the sofa under a thin blanket, and shook his head. “The air conditioning's too high. It's down to twenty degrees in here.” He picked up the remote and adjusted it. “Air-conditioned rooms are dry. Drink plenty of water.”
He went to the window and drew the curtains. “The public walkway is outside. People can see you dressed like that.”
The nightgown sisterhood felt a little embarrassed. They nodded and tugged their gowns down over their thighs to show they accepted the correction.
“Going to play tennis?” his mother asked.

“Yes. I may be back late. I'm meeting some high-school classmates,” he said. “I brewed your herbal medicine. It's in the refrigerator. Don't stop taking it once you've started, or the little bumps will come back on your face.”
“Yes, yes! I remember, good boy. You're getting more and more naggy.” His beautiful thirty-nine-year-old mother bounced up, mussed his hair with both hands, and planted a hard kiss on his cheek.
Naggy? Perhaps that came from the man's genes, Chu Zihang thought.
“As long as you remember.” He turned and went out.

Later he understood why the man had always fretted about something as small as drinking milk. Perhaps he knew what had been lost could never be recovered and dared not ask for it, and only wanted to do something to show the past had not been an illusion, that he still had a connection to it.
It was a long thread leading back to the past. So long as it remained unbroken, perhaps there was still no despair, and he need not give up hope.
“I just can't resist a boy like your son, so poised and never smiling! My eyes are blinded by his radiance!” Auntie Shanshan announced.
“I can't help fangirling... He's too adorable! If I were twenty years younger, I'd carry him right out of your house!” Auntie Annie clutched her chest.
“As if you'd get a turn before me! Yingying, let Zihang be my godson!” Auntie EB shrieked.

“Dream on! How could my son be carried off by old women like you?” His mother's smug voice suddenly turned to giggles. “Oh, stop tickling, stop tickling! I was kidding, kidding! Shanshan, you can be my son's second mom from today, all right? Oh, I shouldn't have told you where I'm ticklish...”
Chu Zihang closed the door behind him, shutting out the women's clamor.

In the garage, beside the Mercedes S500, stood a new car, dark blue, long and low like a sleeping leopard: a Porsche Panamera, his “dad's” new toy. Dad had generously said Chu Zihang could use it whenever he liked. For one thing, Chu Zihang was a good driver, unlikely to damage it; for another, Dad was happy for his stepson to show their wealth and taste to classmates in his busy absence.

Chu Zihang sat in the driver's seat, lowered the sun visor, and studied his face in the mirror: clear lines, a broad forehead, straight nose, strong brows, and gentle black eyes, the face of a good student. He had been born looking like this. Even on a wanted poster, people would mistake his picture for an outstanding-student certificate.

He looked down and removed two soft black films from his eyes: Johnson & Johnson daily disposable cosmetic contacts, the popular Butterfly Black loved by fashionable girls. He closed his eyes, concentrated, and slowly opened them. Light flared in them like torches dropped into an ancient well!

He brushed back his hair and slowly, deliberately worked his facial muscles. The mirror now held another person: a face hard as a glacier, a flickering golden gleam deep in the pupils like will-o'-the-wisps. No one would willingly meet his eyes now. A savage, spear-sharp presence spread soundlessly; looking into those eyes was like having a gun with its safety off pressed between your brows.
Sometimes even Chu Zihang could not tell which was his real self.
He put on black sunglasses. “Start!”

The 4.8-liter V8 roared, the gears of the seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission meshing smoothly and delivering power evenly to all four wheels. The broad tires gripped the ground like a beast's claws curled before a pounce.

The roller door rose slowly. Sunlight poured over the windshield like a waterfall. Chu Zihang released the brake and floored the accelerator. The engine sang, and the Panamera pierced the brilliant curtain of light like a freshly sharpened sword.
